title: Kappa-scale sampling class animation: how do uncertainty classes behave under scaling?
summary: A scale parameter can move a sampling distribution from deterministic to fully random. Three key frames show the cloud of sampled points at three scales, and one curve shows how the output spread grows between a lower limit (zero) and an upper limit (the prior spread).

media.alt: Top: three small square panels, frame 1 kappa 0.1 with a tight teal cluster at a rose plus inside an amber dashed box; frame 2 kappa 1 with a cloud filling the box; frame 3 kappa 10 with a wider cloud extending beyond the box. Bottom: spread against log kappa, an S-shaped teal curve rising from 0 to 1 between a dotted rose line at 0 and a dashed amber line at 1, with three white markers at kappa 0.1, 1 and 10.
media.caption: Reference render of class F8.9 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: How do uncertainty classes behave under scaling?
read_the_figure.axes: Top panels: two parameters, each from about -1.7 to 1.7, with the amber dashed box marking the prior bounds (plus or minus 1). Bottom panel: scale kappa on a logarithmic x axis (0.01 to 100) and relative spread (output standard deviation) from -0.1 to 1.25 on y.
look_at: How does the cloud change from frame to frame, relative to the amber box and the plus?
Where on the curve do the three frames sit, and are they marked on the curve?
Are the two limits (deterministic and prior) drawn, and does the curve approach them?
Is the curve a measurement or a model, and how was the spread defined?
as_drawn: Three frames at kappa = 0.1, 1 and 10 with 300 samples each. The cloud's standard deviation is s = kappa / sqrt(1 + kappa^2): 0.10, 0.71 and 0.995.

The bottom curve is s(kappa): it rises from 0 (dotted rose lower limit, deterministic) to 1 (dashed amber upper limit, prior spread) and flattens above kappa of about 3; the markers (circle, square, triangle) match the frames.
The amber box marks plus or minus 1, the prior half-width, but it is not a bound on the samples: at kappa = 10 about 53 percent of the points lie outside it.
The legend sits over the upper limit line, which hides part of the line near kappa of 0.1 to 10.
read_the_figure.proves: The curve shows, for the stated model, how the sampling spread depends on the scale and that it is confined between the two limits. In this render the curve is a stated formula, not a measurement.
if_wrong: A curve that overshoots the upper limit: the prior spread is not the true maximum, or the scaling is wrong.
Frames not marked on the curve: the reader cannot connect cloud and number.
A box drawn as bounds when it is only a reference: the reader may think samples are truncated.
must_check: UQ limits shown: the two limits define what the scale parameter interpolates between, and every point of the curve is read against them.

terms.meaning: A number that multiplies or interpolates a perturbation; here kappa.
The case of no uncertainty: all samples at one point, spread 0.
The case where the sampling spread equals the full prior spread, normalised to 1.
The standard deviation of the output divided by the prior standard deviation.
A selected snapshot of an animation, here one per scale.
The reference box showing the half-width of the prior; a guide, not a hard limit.

remember: In this render s(kappa) = kappa / sqrt(1 + kappa^2).
Limits: s approaches 0 as kappa goes to 0 and 1 as kappa goes to infinity.
A box on a Gaussian cloud is a reference, not a bound: a standard deviation equal to the half-width puts about 53 percent of the points outside.
Mark the animation's frames on the curve.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: The three upper panels are snapshots of a cloud of sampled points (teal) around the deterministic point (rose plus) with the prior box (amber dashed). The lower panel is the summary: position along the log axis is the scale, height is the spread of the output, and the markers (circle, square, triangle) tie each frame to its place on the curve. The two horizontal lines are the limits.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: imagine a dial that goes from 'no uncertainty' to 'full uncertainty'. As you turn it, the cloud of samples grows. Showing three frames makes the idea concrete, and the curve shows the whole dial at once: slow growth at the start, fast in the middle and a ceiling at the end. The limits tell you the two extremes the model must reproduce, which is how to check that a sampling scheme is right.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A static set of three frames gives no sense of the continuous change; the curve is needed. A box drawn around the cloud suggests that the samples are confined, which they are not: at the largest scale half of them lie outside it. A logarithmic scale compresses the region where the spread is already near 1, so it looks as if the curve stops growing when it is simply saturating. The curve here is a model formula, so its agreement with the limits is by construction.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A plot of the spread against kappa for a real model with error bars would be a measurement. A pair plot of the samples at the largest and smallest scale shows the shape in more dimensions. A table of kappa, spread and fraction outside the box gives the exact numbers.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add the fraction of samples outside the prior box as a second curve, mark kappa = 0.577 where the spread is half, move the legend away from the limit lines, and add an animation slider that moves the markers along the curve.

steps.title: The spread formula
steps.note: The standard deviation of each frame's samples; the limits are 0 and 1.

steps.title: Half-way scale
steps.note: Between frames 1 and 2 on the curve, as the figure shows.

steps.title: Fraction of samples inside the prior box
steps.note: For independent standard normal draws scaled by s; at kappa = 10 about 53 percent are outside the box.

worked.title: Reading the kappa-scale figure of the reference render
worked.problem: (1) What is the output spread at the three frames? (2) At what scale is the spread half of its limit? (3) What fraction of the points of frame 3 lies inside the amber box?

solution.text: (3) Use the probability that both coordinates lie within plus or minus 1 for a standard deviation of 0.995.

worked.answer: Spreads 0.10, 0.71 and 0.995; half the limit at kappa of 0.58; about 47 percent of frame 3's points lie inside the box (53 percent outside), so the box is a reference, not a bound.

analyze.q: The curve approaches 1 above kappa of 3. What does that say about the effect of increasing kappa from 10 to 100?
Why must the limits be drawn on the plot, even though the curve visibly flattens?
analyze.hint: The reader needs the meaning of 0 and 1.

analyze.q: How would you redraw frame 3 so that the box is not misread as a bound?
analyze.hint: Label it, or shade outside points.

evaluate.q: A real sampling scheme gives a curve that exceeds the upper limit. What do you suspect?
evaluate.hint: Definition of the limit, scaling, correlation.

create: Add the fraction of samples outside the prior box as a second curve and label kappa = 0.577.
Redraw the three frames with outside points in a different colour.

checks.q: What do the two limits represent?
checks.answer: The lower limit is the deterministic case (no spread) and the upper limit is the full prior spread; the scale parameter interpolates between them.

checks.q: Half the points of frame 3 lie outside the amber box. Does that mean the sampling violates the prior?
checks.answer: No: the box is a reference half-width of the prior, not a bound; a Gaussian with that standard deviation always puts a large share outside it, so the box should be labelled as a guide and not drawn as a limit.
